Blue mackerel (Scomber australasicus) eggs are pelagic and spherical, drifting in the upper water column until eclosion. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 18.7 °C [T = 18.7 °C], the yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion after four days [ab = four days] of incubation. This brief embryonic period is characteristic of many small-egged scombrids, where rapid development is favoured by warm, productive waters. The newly emerged prolarva is lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, and measures only a few millimetres in total length. Its wet weight at the moment of hatching is approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of about one millimetre. This minimal initial mass underscores the extreme fecundity required by the species, as each female produces vast numbers of such small offspring to offset high early-life mortality. Following yolk-sac resorption, the larvae undergo a trophic switch and commence exogenous feeding, preying upon copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton, beginning a period of rapid somatic growth.

Growth in length proceeds rapidly during the juvenile stage, with individuals reaching approximately 44 centimetres [Li = approximately 44 centimetres] in fork length by the time they approach their asymptotic size. However, the more critical milestone for population dynamics is the fork length at which females attain sexual maturity, which occurs at 23.5 centimetres [Lp = 23.5 centimetres]. This size threshold corresponds roughly to the end of the first year of life for most cohorts in the wild, although growth rates can vary considerably with food availability and water temperature. Reaching this length triggers the onset of vitellogenesis in females and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, marking the transition from an immature, actively growing juvenile to a reproductively viable adult. It is at this point, upon achieving a fork length of 23.5 cm, that young females begin contributing to the spawning stock, a parameter frequently used in fishery stock assessments to evaluate the resilience of the population to harvesting pressure.

The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult blue mackerel is considerable, with large individuals reaching an asymptotic body mass of approximately 1,400 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,400 grams], a value consistent with the typical size range for a mid-level pelagic predator in the productive waters of the western Pacific. Achieving such a mass requires sustained feeding over several years and reflects the species' role as a mid-level pelagic predator. By contrast, the enormous disparity between this final adult mass and the initial wet weight of the newly hatched larva, which is a mere 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], illustrates the extraordinary scope of somatic growth that Scomber australasicus undergoes across its life cycle. This growth trajectory is fuelled by a high metabolic rate and a diet rich in energy-dense prey, enabling the species to accumulate body tissues rapidly during the warm summer months when productivity peaks and feeding opportunities are most abundant.

Longevity in blue mackerel is relatively short compared to many temperate teleosts, with the maximum documented lifespan reaching ten years [am = ten years] when the fish are reared at a thermal regime centred around 18.7 °C [T = 18.7 °C]. This comparatively rapid pace of life, characterised by early maturation, high fecundity, and a modest maximum age, aligns with a life-history strategy typical of many small to medium-sized scombrids that inhabit dynamic, seasonally productive pelagic ecosystems. The mortality schedule is correspondingly steep, driven largely by predation from larger tunas, billfish, and marine mammals, as well as by fishing pressure in commercial trawl and purse-seine fisheries. Individuals that survive past the vulnerable juvenile stage may continue to grow and reproduce for the better part of a decade.

Reproduction in Scomber australasicus occurs via broadcast spawning, with females releasing multiple batches of pelagic eggs over an extended spawning season. Field studies indicate that a single female typically produces around 300,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = around 300,000 eggs per spawning event], a value that scales with body size and individual condition. The frequency of these events is high during the peak summer months, with many females spawning every few days, resulting in an estimated two to three spawning events per week [F_R_i = two to three spawning events per week]. This combination of high batch fecundity and frequent reproductive activity allows the species to fecundate immense numbers of oocytes across a season, ensuring that at least some offspring encounter favourable conditions for survival despite the severe demographic losses that characterise the pelagic larval phase. The total energy invested into reproduction each year is substantial, representing a significant proportion of the female's annual energy budget and constraining further somatic growth in older, reproductively active individuals.
